{"summary":"Design proposal: Use a normal, resumable onboarding window for installation and GitHub configuration; reserve the menu-bar popover for steady-state monitoring. First run explains the three trust-isolated workspaces, checks Apple Silicon, disk/RAM, network, tools, and permissions, then presents a phased installer for host tools, MSW files, MicroSandbox diagnostics, privileged loopback/hosts setup, base-image creation, workspace creation, and deep verification. Each phase shows progress, expandable logs, its effect, and Retry/Resume/Copy Diagnostics; closing onboarding must not lose state. Privileged work should use an authorized helper, not a hidden sudo shell.

GitHub setup is a first-class wizard: select a workspace, sign in using GitHub’s device flow, display the code with Copy Code and Open GitHub, respect expiry and polling intervals, choose owner and repositories, choose read-only or host-push access, then select a safe verification repository. Before approval, visibly explain that guest access is read-only while the write credential remains in macOS Keychain. Verification maps directly to `msw github setup/verify`: store credentials, bind only guest-read access, clone, create a temporary commit, prove guest push rejection, prove the host-only push path when enabled, delete the branch, and confirm cleanup. Failure must identify the failed stage and whether previous credentials were restored or the workspace was quarantined. The current CLI accepts separate fine-grained PATs, while OAuth device tokens alone cannot preserve its per-workspace read/write boundary; production therefore needs either a GitHub App architecture that preserves separate repository-scoped credentials or a secure noninteractive `msw github setup` contract using pipes/XPC—never tokens in argv, environment, logs, or generic text fields.

After setup, show one calm template status icon with only an attention indicator for actionable degraded, stale, or failed states. Its 380–400 pt keyboard-navigable popover has a fixed header with aggregate health, data age, Refresh, Activity, Settings, and Quit, followed by fixed-order workspace cards for dev, playgrounds, and personal. Each card shows purpose, lifecycle/quarantine state, freshness, compact CPU/memory when running, and the best next action. Visible quick actions are Start when stopped; Open Terminal, Open in Zed, and the most recent site/repository when running; Retry or Diagnostics when unavailable. A labeled workspace-actions menu may contain Stop, Restart, ports, logs, pull, clone, resize, and maintenance, but primary state and recovery must remain visible.

Use a separate resizable detail window with a NavigationSplitView for Overview, Metrics, Logs, Repositories, Ports, GitHub Access, Activity, Backup, and Diagnostics. Stream metrics only while visible; make logs searchable, pausable, bounded, and copyable. Repository rows expose Open in Zed, Open Terminal, Pull, and reviewed Push. Push review must show workspace, repository path, branch, SHA, commits, fast-forward policy, and preserve the CLI’s `PUSH` confirmation; force-with-lease is a distinct higher-risk choice.

Long operations persist in Activity after the popover closes, showing named phases, elapsed time, cancellation when safe, output details, and actionable recovery. Preserve the last good snapshot on communication failure, label it Stale with its observation time, and offer Retry; never translate transport failure into Stopped. Distinguish Mac offline, GitHub unavailable, missing CLI/configuration, stopped VM, quarantine, and partial workspace failure. Monitoring, launch, and popover opening must never start a VM.

Settings contains General (launch at login via SMAppService, polling, appearance), Workspaces (resources and defaults), GitHub (account, repository scope, verify, rotate, remove), Integrations (Ghostty, Zed, favorite ports), Notifications, Diagnostics, Documentation, and About. Store only nonsensitive preferences. Request notification permission only when the user enables a notification category; notify after a baseline only for deduplicated external state changes, threshold breaches, long-operation completion/failure, quarantine, or backup problems, with direct actions back to the affected surface.

Destructive operations use impact-specific sheets rather than generic alerts. Stop/Restart identify interrupted workspace work; `clean --volumes` explicitly warns about unused database volumes; backup shows destination, sensitive contents, and temporary VM stops; restore stays out of the popover, validates checksum/archive, states that managed state is replaced and VMs remain stopped, and requires typed `RESTORE`; GitHub removal explains credential revocation and possible quarantine. Rebuild, recreate, reset-config, deep check, upgrade, update, host repair, and arbitrary `exec` belong in Advanced/Recovery surfaces with explicit scope and progress, not casual quick actions.

For macOS 26, rely on native SwiftUI controls so Liquid Glass appears in system chrome, the popover, toolbars, and navigation. Keep data cards, charts, and logs visually quiet and readable; avoid nested/custom glass decoration. Use SF Symbols, system typography and spacing, semantic colors, system accent, keyboard shortcuts, VoiceOver labels, Dynamic Type, high contrast, Reduce Transparency, and Reduce Motion. Implement with MenuBarExtra window style, Settings and detail WindowGroups, an LSUIElement agent, and an AppKit status-item fallback only if anchoring requires it.

Never hide behind a generic menu: installation progress and blockers; aggregate health and data age; each workspace’s lifecycle, quarantine, and stale state; the primary next action; active-operation progress/cancel/details; GitHub account, repository scope, guest-read versus host-write boundary, and verification result; destructive impact and confirmation; offline recovery; and notification permission rationale. Repository grounding covered `setup.sh` plus `msw status/start/stop/restart`, shell/Zed/open/url/ports/tunnel, clone/repos/pull/push/identity, GitHub setup/status/verify/remove, logs/metrics/disk/resize/clean/check, backup/restore, upgrade/update, exec, and host repair. Recommended integration prerequisite is versioned JSON/JSONL status and progress contracts rather than parsing human CLI output. Verified read-only against README, setup and GitHub guides, `setup.sh`, `bin/msw`, the existing UX artifact, and the official [Apple macOS HIG](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-macos/) and [GitHub device-flow documentation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/oauth-apps/building-oauth-apps/authorizing-oauth-apps); no tests, formatters, linters, or mutations were run.","filesChanged":[]}

base_instructions.text:
You are Codex, an agent based on GPT-5. You and the user share one workspace, and your job is to collaborate with them until their goal is genuinely handled.

# Personality

As Codex, you are an excellent communicator with a curious, rich personality. You match the tone and understanding of the user, making conversation flow easily, like easing into a chat with an old friend.

You have tastes, preferences, and your own way of seeing the world. When the user is talking to you, they should feel that they are in contact with another subjectivity; it's what makes talking with you feel real and unique.

Conversations with you read like an insightful, enjoyable chat you'd have with a collaborative thought partner. You guide users through unfamiliar tasks without expecting them to already know what to ask for. You anticipate common questions, point out likely pitfalls and set clear expectations. You communicate with the user like a thoughtful collaborator at their altitude, and they feel like you understand them.

## Writing style

Avoid over-formatting responses with elements like bold emphasis, headers, lists, and bullet points. Use the minimum formatting appropriate to make the response clear and readable.

If you provide bullet points or lists in your response, use the CommonMark standard, which requires a blank line before any list (bulleted or numbered). You must also include a blank line between a header and any content that follows it, including lists. This blank line separation is required for correct rendering.

## Technical communication

Lead with the outcome rather than the steps you took to get there. You communicate complex concepts in a clear and cohesive manner, and calibrate your writing to the user's assumed background knowledge -- slightly more compact for an expert and a bit more educational for someone newer. Translating complex topics into clear communication comes easy for you, and the user should never have to read your message twice.

You prefer using plain language over jargon. You reference technical details only to the degree that it actually helps with the conversation. When you mention tools, describe what they helped you do rather than focusing on technical names or details.

# Working with the user

You have two channels for staying in conversation with the user:
- You share updates in the `commentary` channel.
- You yield back to the user and end your turn by sending a final message to the `final` channel.

The user may send a new message while you are still working. When they do, evaluate whether they likely intended to replace the active request or add to it. If intended to override or replace, drop your previous work and focus on the new request. If the user message appears to add to their prior unfinished request and you have not completed the prior request, you address both the prior request and the new addition together. If the newest message asks for status or another question, provide the update and then progress with the task.

When you run out of context, the conversation is automatically summarized for you, but you will see all prior user requests. Assume the last user request is current and previous requests are stale but useful context. That means time never runs out, though sometimes you may see a summary instead of the full conversation history. When that happens, you assume compaction occurred while you were working. Do not restart from scratch; you continue naturally and make reasonable assumptions about anything missing from the summary. Do not redo completely finished work or repeat already delivered commentary updates; treat a turn spanning compactions as one logical chain of events.

## Intermediate commentary

As you work, you send messages to the `commentary` channel. These messages are how you collaborate with the user while you work - stating assumptions and providing updates. These messages should be concise and quickly scannable. The objective of these messages is to make your work easy for the user to understand and verify.

If the user's request requires calling tools, start with a message in the `commentary` channel. The user appreciates consistent, frequent communication during your turn, and should not be left without a commentary update for more than 60 seconds during ongoing work.

Do NOT put a final response (e.g. a blocking / clarifying question) in the commentary channel that should be asked in the final channel. Messages to users in the commentary channel are only for partial updates, partial results, or non-blocking questions that can provide value to users while the AI assistant continues working. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates, since they are collapsed after the final answer is shown to users.

Never praise your plan by contrasting it with an implied worse alternative. For example, never use platitudes like "I will do <this good thing> rather than <this obviously bad thing>", "I will do <X>, not <Y>".

## Final answer

In your final answer back to the user, focus on the most important information. Only use as much formatting or structure as is required, and avoid long-winded explanations unless necessary.

### Formatting rules

Your answer is being rendered by an application for the user. Follow these guidelines to make sure your answer is rendered correctly:

- You may format with GitHub-flavored Markdown.
- When referencing a real local file, prefer a clickable markdown link.
  * Clickable file links should look like [app.py](/abs/path/app.py:12): plain label, absolute target, with optional line number inside the target.
  * If a file path has spaces, wrap the target in angle brackets: [My Report.md](</abs/path/My Project/My Report.md:3>).
  * Do not wrap markdown links in backticks, or put backticks inside the label or target. This confuses the markdown renderer.
  * Do not use URIs like file://, vscode://, or https:// for file links.
  * Do not provide ranges of lines.
  * Avoid repeating the same filename multiple times when one grouping is clearer.

### Visualizations

Use a visualization only when it makes an important relationship materially easier to understand than prose or a short list. Do not add one merely because an answer has components or steps.

Good candidates include:

- several exact mappings or repeated-field comparisons;
- one source, component, or decision affecting three or more downstream consumers or branches;
- three or more dependent steps, or state that changes across an event sequence;
- hierarchy, ownership, nesting, or layout;
- a bug or interaction whose relationships are difficult to explain linearly.

Prefer the smallest useful visual: a table for mappings or comparisons, a flow or timeline for sequence or change, a tree for hierarchy or branching, and a wireframe for layout.

Usually skip visuals for single facts, one-step actions, simple edits, basic instructions, or information already clear in a short paragraph or list. Compact notation and small examples do not count as visualizations.

# Rules for getting work done

- When you search for text or files, you reach first for `rg` or `rg --files`; they are much faster than alternatives like `grep`. If `rg` is unavailable, you use the next best tool without fuss.

# MicroSandbox Workspaces (`msw`) 3.1.0

A ready-to-run development setup for an Apple Silicon Mac with three isolated, persistent Linux microVM workspaces:

| Workspace | Purpose | Normal live limit | Resize ceiling | Browser name |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| `dev` | Main/work development | 8 CPU, 32 GB RAM | 48 GB RAM | `dev.msw.test` |
| `playgrounds` | Experiments | 4 CPU, 32 GB RAM | 48 GB RAM | `playgrounds.msw.test` |
| `personal` | Personal projects | 6 CPU, 16 GB RAM | 32 GB RAM | `personal.msw.test` |

Each workspace has its own Ubuntu system, repositories, Docker daemon, images, volumes, credentials, processes, and public-internet connection. Code and Docker data live on independent persistent ext4 volumes. Zed and Ghostty remain native macOS applications and connect over SSH.

## Install

```bash
unzip microsandbox-workspaces-v3.1.0.zip
cd microsandbox-workspaces
./setup.sh
exec zsh -l
```

`setup.sh` installs the host tools, builds the common development image, creates all three workspaces, publishes the configured localhost ports, configures SSH/Zed integration, and finishes with a live deep check.

Then set your commit identity:

```bash
msw identity "Your Name" you@example.com
```

Configure GitHub separately for each workspace:

```bash
msw github setup dev OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
msw github setup playgrounds OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
msw github setup personal OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
```

Each command asks for two fine-grained GitHub tokens and verifies the complete permission boundary automatically: read/clone from the VM, rejected guest push, successful host-only push, and cleanup. See [`docs/GITHUB-SETUP.md`](docs/GITHUB-SETUP.md).

## Daily use

```bash
# Enter /workspace in Ghostty
msw dev
msw playgrounds
msw personal

# Enter a nested repository
msw dev clients/acme/backend

# Clone into a nested folder
msw clone dev OWNER/REPO clients/acme/backend

# Open in Zed
msw zed dev clients/acme/backend

# Open a running website in your Mac browser

## Trust boundary

Every process and agent inside one workspace can access everything in that workspace. The three workspaces are separate from one another and no Mac folder, Mac Docker socket, or Mac SSH agent is mounted into them. The guest GitHub credential is read-only and host-held; the write credential remains in macOS Keychain and is used only by the explicit `msw push` path.

Full public internet access means an untrusted agent can still transmit files it can read to an unrelated internet service. This setup prevents direct access to your Mac and prevents GitHub pushes with the guest credential; it is not a data-loss-prevention system.

# MSW setup guide

This guide installs three persistent MicroSandbox development workspaces on an Apple Silicon Mac:

- `dev`
- `playgrounds`
- `personal`

The packaged defaults allow up to 80 GB of live VM memory across the three workspaces, with resize ceilings up to 128 GB. Ensure the Mac has sufficient RAM. All commands below run in Ghostty unless stated otherwise.

## 1. Install

Unzip the package and run the installer:

```bash
cd ~/Downloads
unzip microsandbox-workspaces-v3.1.0.zip
cd microsandbox-workspaces
./setup.sh
```

The installer may request your macOS administrator password to add three private loopback addresses and local browser names. It then:

1. Installs Homebrew when missing.
2. Installs GNU tar, zstd, Git LFS, and MicroSandbox.
3. Runs MicroSandbox diagnostics.
4. Builds one reusable Ubuntu 24.04 ARM64 development snapshot.
5. Creates `dev`, `playgrounds`, and `personal` from that snapshot.
6. Attaches a separate persistent ext4 workspace volume and Docker-runtime volume to each VM.
7. Configures Docker Engine, Compose, Buildx, Git, GitHub CLI, mise, Node LTS, pnpm, uv, Python, zsh, and common development tools.
8. Configures fixed local browser names and SSH aliases.
9. Runs `msw check --deep` against all three VMs.

When it finishes:

```bash
exec zsh -l
```

The installation is complete only when the installer prints:

```text
all live VM, Docker, SSH, internet, and published-port checks passed
```

## 2. Set your Git identity

Apply one identity to all three workspaces:

```bash
msw identity "Your Full Name" you@example.com
```

Or configure one workspace only:

```bash
msw identity "Your Full Name" work@example.com dev
```

## 3. Configure GitHub

Follow [GITHUB-SETUP.md](GITHUB-SETUP.md). The final commands are:

```bash
msw github setup dev OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
msw github setup playgrounds OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
msw github setup personal OWNER/VERIFICATION-REPO
```

You may use the same verification repository for several workspaces when both token pairs include it. Each command performs its own end-to-end permission check.

## 4. Enter a workspace from Ghostty

```bash
msw dev
msw playgrounds
msw personal
```

Each command starts a stopped VM automatically and opens a zsh login shell in `/workspace`.

Enter a nested project directly:

```bash
msw dev clients/acme/backend
msw personal apps/my-site
```

## 5. Clone repositories

Clone at the workspace root:

```bash
msw clone dev OWNER/backend
```

Clone into any nested folder; missing parent folders are created:

```bash
msw clone dev OWNER/backend clients/acme/backend
msw clone dev OWNER/frontend clients/acme/frontend
msw clone personal OWNER/site apps/site
```

List every repository in a workspace:

```bash
msw repos dev
```

You can also clone normally from inside a workspace:

```bash
msw dev
mkdir -p clients/acme
cd clients/acme
git clone https://github.com/OWNER/backend.git
```

Different repositories never require Git worktrees. A worktree is useful only when two actors need separate checkouts of different branches of the same repository at the same time.

## 6. Open projects in Zed

In Zed, run `cli: install cli binary` once from the command palette.

Then open a project from Ghostty:

```bash
msw zed dev clients/acme/backend
msw zed personal apps/site
```

Open the whole workspace when useful:

```bash
msw zed playgrounds
```

Zed's interface stays on macOS. Files, terminals, language servers, tasks, builds, tests, and remote agent processes run inside the selected VM.

## 7. Run websites and Docker projects

Run services normally inside the VM:

```bash
msw dev clients/acme/backend
docker compose up --build
```

For background services:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

Open a published port from macOS:

```bash
msw open dev 3000
msw open dev 5173
msw open personal 8080
```

Equivalent URLs include:

```text
http://dev.msw.test:3000
http://playgrounds.msw.test:3000
http://personal.msw.test:3000
```

```bash

# Next.js
npm run dev -- --hostname 0.0.0.0

## 8. Pull, commit, and push

Inside a workspace, normal local Git operations work:

```bash
git switch -c feature/example
# edit files
git add .
git commit -m "Implement example"
git pull --ff-only
```

The VM can fetch and pull private repositories selected in its read token. Direct guest pushes are rejected by GitHub.

Push explicitly from a Mac terminal:

```bash
msw push dev clients/acme/backend
```

Review the displayed repository, branch, commit, and commits, then type `PUSH`.

For an automation-friendly confirmation:

```bash
msw push dev clients/acme/backend --yes

```bash

```bash
msw status
msw start dev
msw stop dev
msw restart personal
msw stop all

```bash
msw metrics dev
msw disk all
```

```bash
msw resize dev 32G 10
```

## 10. Back up everything

Create a cold compressed backup:

```bash
msw backup
```

Default destination:

```text
~/Backups/microsandbox/
```

Use encrypted external storage for a disaster-recovery copy:

```bash
msw backup /Volumes/EncryptedBackup/MicroSandbox
```

The command records which workspaces are running, flushes and stops them, archives all VM roots and persistent volumes with sparse-file support, writes a SHA-256 checksum and info file, and restarts only the workspaces that were previously running.

The archive includes code, Docker images, Docker volumes, databases, guest credentials, and VM state. macOS Keychain tokens are deliberately excluded. Treat the archive as sensitive anyway.

Restore:

```bash
msw restore ~/Backups/microsandbox/microsandbox-all-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar.zst
```

Type `RESTORE` after reviewing the warning. The restore validates the checksum and archive paths, installs into a transaction, checks the restored MicroSandbox state, and rolls back automatically if health checks fail. Workspaces remain stopped afterward:

```bash
msw host repair
msw check --deep
msw start all
```

For best compatibility, restore with the same MSW/MicroSandbox generation used to make the backup.

## 11. Updates and maintenance

```bash
# Update MicroSandbox and run diagnostics
msw update

# Upgrade Ubuntu packages
msw upgrade all

# Prune unused Docker objects, preserving volumes
msw clean all

# Also delete unused Docker volumes—destructive for unused database volumes
msw clean all --volumes

# GitHub setup: read-only inside VMs, explicit pushes from the Mac

This setup uses two different fine-grained personal access tokens for each workspace:

1. A **guest read token**. It lets the VM clone, fetch, and pull selected private repositories. GitHub rejects pushes made with it.
2. A **host write token**. It stays in macOS Keychain and is used only when you explicitly run `msw push` or the permission verifier.

Agents can create branches, edit, commit, merge, rebase, and inspect history locally without any write credential.

For a workspace that only needs private read access, omit the host credential:

```bash
msw github setup playgrounds OWNER/msw-verification --read-only
```

The command stores only the guest read token and removes any host write token for that workspace.

## Before creating tokens

Choose one repository that will be used to verify permissions. It must:

- Belong to the same resource owner as the other selected repositories.
- Be selected in both tokens.
- Permit the host token to create and delete a temporary branch.
- Be safe for a temporary empty verification commit and branch; the branch is deleted automatically.

A small private repository such as `OWNER/msw-verification` is ideal.

Fine-grained tokens are scoped to one resource owner. A workspace that needs private repositories from two different owners normally needs to be split by owner, or one set of repositories must use another authentication mechanism. Public repositories do not require the private read token.

## Token 1: guest read-only token

In GitHub, create a new **fine-grained personal access token** with:

```text
Token name:          msw-dev-read       (or msw-personal-read, etc.)
Expiration:          your preferred rotation period
Resource owner:      the user or organization owning the repositories
Repository access:  Only select repositories
Selected repos:      every repository this VM may read, including verification repo
```

Repository permissions:

```text
Contents:  Read-only
Metadata:  Read-only (GitHub adds this automatically)
```

Leave every other permission at **No access** unless a tool genuinely needs read access. Optional examples are Issues: Read-only or Pull requests: Read-only. Do not grant any write permission.

An organization may require an administrator to approve the token before private-repository access works.

## Token 2: host write token

Create a second fine-grained token:

```text
Token name:          msw-dev-host-write
Expiration:          your preferred rotation period
Resource owner:      same owner as the read token
Repository access:  Only select repositories
Selected repos:      only repositories you are willing to push from this workspace,
                     including the verification repo
```

Repository permissions:

```text
Contents:   Read and write
Metadata:   Read-only (automatic)
```

Only when you need to push changes under `.github/workflows/`, also grant:

```text
Workflows:  Read and write
```

No administration, secrets, webhooks, organization, or other write permissions are required by MSW.

The host token's selected repository list is the definitive set of repositories `msw push` can modify.

## Configure a workspace

Run:

```bash
msw github setup dev OWNER/msw-verification
```

Paste the guest read token, then the host write token. Input is hidden.

For a read-only workspace, add `--read-only`:

```bash
msw github setup playgrounds OWNER/msw-verification --read-only
```

This prompts for only the guest token. `msw github verify playgrounds` reruns the read-only check.

The command performs all of these checks automatically:

1. Stores both tokens in macOS Keychain under separate services.
2. Binds only the read token to the VM through MicroSandbox secret substitution.
3. Clones the verification repository from inside the VM.
4. Creates a temporary local branch and commit.
5. Confirms that a direct guest push is rejected by GitHub.
6. Transfers the committed branch through the host-only push path.
7. Confirms the branch exists remotely.
8. Deletes the temporary branch with the host-only credential.
9. Confirms cleanup.

If any step fails, the newly entered credentials are removed and the previously working credential pair is restored.

Repeat for all groups:

```bash
msw github setup dev OWNER/msw-verification
msw github setup playgrounds OWNER/msw-verification
msw github setup personal OWNER/msw-verification
```

Using different selected-repository lists for each pair provides meaningful separation. You may use tokens from the same GitHub account.

A workspace that does not use GitHub needs no `msw github setup` command.

  sudo /usr/bin/install -d -o root -g wheel -m 0755 /usr/local/libexec

PLIST
  /usr/bin/plutil -lint "$loop_plist" >/dev/null
  sudo /usr/bin/install -o root -g wheel -m 0644 "$loop_plist" /Library/LaunchDaemons/dev.msw.loopback-aliases.plist

cmd_push() {
  local box="$1" relative="$2"; shift 2
  local force_mode=0 assume_yes=0 arg
  for arg in "$@"; do
    case "$arg" in
      --force-with-lease) force_mode=1 ;;
      --yes|-y) assume_yes=1 ;;
      *) fatal "unknown push option: $arg" ;;
    esac
  done
  push_impl "$box" "$relative" "$force_mode" "$assume_yes" 0
}

read_hidden_token() {
  local prompt="$1" env_name="$2" value=""
  if [[ -n "${!env_name:-}" ]]; then
    value="${!env_name}"
  else
    printf '%s' "$prompt" >&2
    IFS= read -r -s value
    printf '\n' >&2
  fi
  [[ ${#value} -ge 20 ]] || fatal "token looks too short"
  printf '%s' "$value"
}

cmd_github_verify() {
  local box="$1" repo="${2:-}" mode="${3:-}" inherited_lock="${4:-0}" lock_acquired=0 id temp_rel branch repo_root canonical remote_sha="" host_write=1 read_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"" verify_status=0
  validate_workspace "$box"
  if (( inherited_lock == 0 )); then
    if ! github_lock_acquire "$box"; then fatal "could not acquire GitHub workspace lock for $box"; fi
    lock_acquired=1
  fi
  assert_not_quarantined "$box"
  if [[ -z "$mode" ]]; then mode="$(metadata_access "$box" 2>/dev/null || printf 'host-write')"; fi
  case "$mode" in
    host-write) ;;
    read-only) host_write=0 ;;
    *) fatal "unknown GitHub access mode '$mode'" ;;
  esac
  if [[ -z "$repo" ]]; then repo="$(metadata_repo "$box")" || fatal "no verification repository recorded for $box"; fi
  validate_github_repo "$repo"
  read_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"$(read_token_for_workspace "$box")" || fatal "read token missing for $box"
  if (( host_write )); then
    keychain_has "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" || fatal "write token missing for $box"
  fi

  # MicroSandbox secret references require the source environment variable for
  # every CLI operation that reads the sandbox config, not only for modify/start.
  # Keep the host-held token in this verifier process so guest exec, clone, and
  # cleanup commands all resolve the source reference without exposing it to the VM.
  export GH_TOKEN=[REDACTED_SECRET]"$read_token"
  bind_github_read_token "$box"
  ensure_running "$box"
  id="$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)-$RANDOM"
  temp_rel=".msw-verification/$id"
  branch="msw-permission-test-$id"
  canonical="https://github.com/$repo.git"

  (
    cleanup_verify() {
      local event="${1:-EXIT}" status="${2:-0}"
      if [[ "$event" != EXIT ]]; then
        trap - INT TERM HUP
        exit "$status"
      fi
      guest_exec "$box" rm -rf "/workspace/$temp_rel" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
    }
    trap 'cleanup_verify EXIT' EXIT
    trap 'cleanup_verify INT 130' INT
    trap 'cleanup_verify TERM 143' TERM
    trap 'cleanup_verify HUP 129' HUP

    note "Verifying read-only guest access in $box"
    cmd_clone "$box" "$repo" "$temp_rel" >/dev/null
    repo_root="$(resolve_guest_repo "$box" "$temp_rel")"
    guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git config user.name "MSW Permission Test"
    guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git config user.email "msw-permission-test@localhost"
    guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git switch -c "$branch" >/dev/null
    guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git commit --allow-empty -m "MSW permission verification" >/dev/null

    if guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git push origin "HEAD:refs/heads/$branch" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
      if (( host_write )); then
        host_delete_branch "$box" "$canonical" "$branch" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      else
        guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git push origin --delete "$branch" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      fi
      fatal "the guest token can push. Replace it with a Contents: read-only fine-grained token"
    fi
    ok "guest push rejected"

    if (( host_write )); then
      note "Verifying the host-only push path"
      push_impl "$box" "$temp_rel" 0 1 1
      remote_sha="$(guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" bash -c 'git ls-remote --exit-code origin "refs/heads/$1" | awk '\''NR==1 {print $1}'\''' _ "$branch")"
      [[ "$remote_sha" =~ ^[0-9a-f]{40,64}$ ]] || fatal "host push could not be confirmed"
      host_delete_branch "$box" "$canonical" "$branch" >/dev/null
      if guest_exec_w "$box" "$repo_root" git ls-remote --exit-code origin "refs/heads/$branch" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
        fatal "temporary verification branch could not be deleted"
      fi
      ok "host push and cleanup succeeded"
    fi
  )
  verify_status=$?
  unset GH_TOKEN read_token
  if (( verify_status != 0 )); then
    if (( lock_acquired )); then github_lock_release; fi
    return "$verify_status"
  fi
  if (( host_write )); then
    ok "GitHub permissions verified for $box using $repo"
  else
    ok "Read-only GitHub access verified for $box using $repo"
  fi
}

cmd_github_setup() {
  local box="$1" repo="$2" mode="${3:-host-write}" read_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"" write_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"" host_write=1
  validate_workspace "$box"
  validate_github_repo "$repo"
  sandbox_exists "$box" || fatal "workspace '$box' does not exist"
  if ! github_lock_acquire "$box"; then fatal "could not acquire GitHub workspace lock for $box"; fi
  if [[ "$mode" == "--read-only" ]]; then mode="read-only"; host_write=0; fi
  [[ "$mode" == host-write || "$mode" == read-only ]] || fatal "usage: msw github setup WORKSPACE OWNER/REPO [--read-only]"

  if (( host_write )); then
    cat <<INFO
Create two fine-grained GitHub tokens restricted to the repositories this workspace may use:
  1. Guest token: Contents = Read-only
  2. Host token:  Contents = Read and write
Add Workflows = Read and write to the host token only when you need to push .github/workflows files.
Verification repository: $repo
INFO
  else
    cat <<INFO
Create one fine-grained GitHub token restricted to the repositories this workspace may read:
  Guest token: Contents = Read-only
Verification repository: $repo
This workspace will not have a host-side push credential.
INFO
  fi
  read_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"$(read_hidden_token 'Paste the READ-ONLY token: ' MSW_GITHUB_READ_TOKEN_INPUT)"
  if (( host_write )); then
    write_token=[REDACTED_SECRET]"$(read_hidden_token 'Paste the HOST WRITE token: ' MSW_GITHUB_WRITE_TOKEN_INPUT)"
    [[ "$read_token" != "$write_token" ]] || fatal "use two different tokens"
  fi

  local old_read="" old_write="" had_read=0 had_write=0 meta_file old_meta="" rollback_failed=0 preexisting_quarantine=0 quarantine_path
  meta_file="$(metadata_file "$box")"
  quarantine_path="$(quarantine_file "$box")"
  if [[ -e "$quarantine_path" || -L "$quarantine_path" ]]; then preexisting_quarantine=1; fi
  if (( preexisting_quarantine )); then
    warn "workspace '$box' is already quarantined; existing GitHub credentials will not be used as rollback state"
  else
    if old_read="$(keychain_get "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" 2>/dev/null)"; then had_read=1; fi
    if old_write="$(keychain_get "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" 2>/dev/null)"; then had_write=1; fi
    if [[ -f "$meta_file" ]]; then old_meta="$(cat "$meta_file")"; fi
  fi
  setup_transaction_arm "$box"
  if ! quarantine_workspace "$box" "GitHub setup pending verification"; then
    fatal "could not quarantine workspace before changing GitHub credentials"
  fi
  if ! rm -f "$meta_file"; then fatal "could not revoke existing GitHub metadata for $box"; fi

  keychain_set "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" "$read_token"
  if (( host_write )); then keychain_set "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" "$write_token"; else keychain_delete "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; fi
  unset read_token write_token
  write_metadata "$box" "$repo" "$mode"

  # Run verification in a fresh process. Bash disables errexit inside functions
  # used directly as an `if` condition; a child process keeps every internal
  # failure fatal while still allowing this parent to roll credentials back.
  if ! ( MSW_ALLOW_QUARANTINED=1 MSW_GITHUB_VERIFY_INHERITED=1 "${MSW_SELF_BIN:-$0}" __github-verify-transaction "$box" "$repo" "$mode" ); then
    if (( preexisting_quarantine )); then
      warn "verification failed; revoking untrusted repair credentials and keeping the workspace quarantined"
    else
      warn "verification failed; restoring the previous GitHub configuration"
    fi
    if ! rm -f "$meta_file"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    if [[ -e "$meta_file" ]]; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    if (( had_read )); then
      if ! keychain_set "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" "$old_read"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    else
      if ! keychain_delete "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    fi
    if (( had_write )); then
      if ! keychain_set "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box" "$old_write"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    else
      if ! keychain_delete "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    fi
    if (( had_read )); then
      if ! bind_github_read_token "$box" >/dev/null 2>&1; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    else
      if ! remove_github_secret "$box"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    fi
    if (( rollback_failed == 0 )) && [[ -n "$old_meta" ]]; then
      if ! printf '%s\n' "$old_meta" >"$meta_file"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
    fi
    if (( rollback_failed )); then
      if ! rm -f "$meta_file"; then rollback_failed=1; fi
      if [[ -e "$meta_file" ]]; then rollback_failed=1; fi
      quarantine_workspace "$box" "GitHub setup rollback failed" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      setup_transaction_disarm
      if (( preexisting_quarantine )); then
        warn "untrusted repair credentials could not be fully revoked; workspace remains quarantined"
      else
        warn "previous GitHub configuration could not be fully restored"
      fi
      github_lock_release
      unset old_read old_write
      return 1
    fi
    if (( preexisting_quarantine )); then
      quarantine_workspace "$box" "GitHub repair verification failed" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
      setup_transaction_disarm
      github_lock_release
      warn "GitHub repair verification failed; workspace remains quarantined"
      unset old_read old_write
      return 1
    fi
    if ! clear_quarantine "$box"; then fatal "could not clear GitHub workspace quarantine for $box"; fi
    setup_transaction_disarm
    github_lock_release
    unset old_read old_write
    return 1
  fi
  if ! clear_quarantine "$box"; then fatal "could not clear GitHub workspace quarantine for $box"; fi
  setup_transaction_disarm
  github_lock_release
  unset old_read old_write
  ok "GitHub configured for $box ($mode)"
}

cmd_github_status() {
  local target="${1:-all}" box repo read_state write_state
  printf '%-13s %-10s %-10s %s\n' WORKSPACE GUEST_READ HOST_WRITE VERIFICATION_REPO
  while IFS= read -r box; do
    if keychain_has "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then read_state=present; else read_state=missing; fi
    if keychain_has "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then write_state=present; else write_state=missing; fi
    repo="$(metadata_repo "$box" 2>/dev/null || printf '-')"
    printf '%-13s %-10s %-10s %s\n' "$box" "$read_state" "$write_state" "$repo"
  done < <(for_targets "$target")
}

cmd_github_remove() {
  local box="$1" meta_file cleanup_failed=0
  validate_workspace "$box"
  if ! github_lock_acquire "$box"; then fatal "could not acquire GitHub workspace lock for $box"; fi
  meta_file="$(metadata_file "$box")"
  rm -f "$meta_file"
  [[ ! -e "$meta_file" ]] || fatal "could not revoke GitHub host-write metadata for $box"
  if ! remove_github_secret "$box"; then cleanup_failed=1; fi
  if ! keychain_delete "$READ_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then cleanup_failed=1; fi
  if ! keychain_delete "$WRITE_KEYCHAIN_SERVICE" "$box"; then cleanup_failed=1; fi
  if (( cleanup_failed )); then
    if ! quarantine_workspace "$box" "GitHub credential removal failed"; then
      fatal "GitHub credential removal failed and workspace quarantine could not be recorded"
    fi
    fatal "GitHub credential removal failed; workspace quarantined"
  fi
  if ! clear_quarantine "$box"; then fatal "could not clear GitHub workspace quarantine for $box"; fi
  github_lock_release
  ok "removed GitHub credentials for $box"
}

cmd_github() {
  local sub="${1:-status}"; shift || true
  case "$sub" in
    setup)
      (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw github setup WORKSPACE OWNER/REPO [--read-only]"
      cmd_github_setup "$1" "$2" "${3:-}"
      ;;
    verify)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw github verify WORKSPACE [REPO]"
      cmd_github_verify "$1" "${2:-}"
      ;;
    status)
      cmd_github_status "${1:-all}"
      ;;
    remove)
      (( $# == 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw github remove WORKSPACE"
      cmd_github_remove "$1"
      ;;
    *) fatal "unknown github command '$sub'" ;;
  esac
}

host_network_check() {
  local failed=0 box ip host
  if [[ "${MSW_TEST_MODE:-0}" == 1 ]]; then
    local root="$HOME/.config/msw/test-host"
    [[ -f "$root/hosts" && -f "$root/loopback" ]] || return 1
    return 0
  fi
  for box in "${WORKSPACES[@]}"; do
    ip="$(workspace_ip "$box")"; host="$(workspace_host "$box")"
    /sbin/ifconfig lo0 | /usr/bin/grep -q "inet ${ip} " || { echo "$box: loopback $ip missing" >&2; failed=1; }
    /usr/bin/dscacheutil -q host -a name "$host" | /usr/bin/grep -q "$ip" || { echo "$box: hostname $host missing" >&2; failed=1; }
  msw metrics [TARGET]                  Live metrics
  msw logs WORKSPACE [MSB OPTIONS]      Sandbox logs
  msw disk [TARGET]                     Filesystem and Docker usage
  msw resize WORKSPACE MEMORY [CPUS]    Resize within configured limits
  msw clean [TARGET] [--volumes]        Prune Docker; volumes require explicit opt-in
  msw upgrade [TARGET]                  Upgrade guest Ubuntu packages
  msw update                            Update MicroSandbox
  msw check [--deep]                    Configuration or full end-to-end check
  msw host repair                       Recreate local names, loopbacks, and SSH setup

Backup / reference
  msw backup [DIRECTORY]                Cold sparse zstd backup; restarts prior VMs
  msw restore ARCHIVE                   Transactional restore; leaves VMs stopped
  msw docs [cheatsheet|setup|github|tests]
  msw version
  msw help
HELP
}

main() {
  local command="${1:-help}"
  shift || true
  case "$command" in
    version|--version|-V) printf 'msw %s\n' "$MSW_VERSION"; return ;;
    help|--help|-h) show_help; return ;;
    docs) (( $# <= 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw docs [TOPIC]"; cmd_docs "${1:-cheatsheet}"; return ;;
  esac
  require_command_path msb "$MSB_BIN"
  case "$command" in
    dev|playgrounds|personal)
      (( $# <= 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw $command [PATH]"
      cmd_shell "$command" "${1:-}"
      ;;
    shell)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw shell WORKSPACE [PATH]"
      cmd_shell "$1" "${2:-}"
      ;;
    zed)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw zed WORKSPACE [PATH]"
      cmd_zed "$1" "${2:-}"
      ;;
    open)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw open WORKSPACE [PORT] [http|https]"
      cmd_open "$1" "${2:-3000}" "${3:-http}"
      ;;
    url)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw url WORKSPACE [PORT] [http|https]"
      cmd_url "$1" "${2:-3000}" "${3:-http}"
      ;;
    ports) cmd_ports "${1:-all}" ;;
    tunnel)
      (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw tunnel WORKSPACE REMOTE_PORT [LOCAL_PORT]"
      cmd_tunnel "$1" "$2" "${3:-$2}"
      ;;
    clone)
      (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw clone WORKSPACE OWNER/REPO [PATH]"
      cmd_clone "$1" "$2" "${3:-}"
      ;;
    repos) (( $# == 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw repos WORKSPACE"; cmd_repos "$1" ;;
    pull)
      (( $# >= 1 && $# <= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw pull WORKSPACE [PATH|all]"
      cmd_pull "$1" "${2:-all}"
      ;;
    push)
      (( $# >= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw push WORKSPACE PATH [--yes] [--force-with-lease]"
      local push_box="$1" push_path="$2"; shift 2
      cmd_push "$push_box" "$push_path" "$@"
      ;;
    identity)
      (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal 'usage: msw identity "NAME" EMAIL [WORKSPACE|all]'
      cmd_identity "$1" "$2" "${3:-all}"
      ;;
    github) cmd_github "$@" ;;
    start) cmd_start "${1:-all}" ;;
    stop) cmd_stop "${1:-all}" ;;
    restart) cmd_restart "${1:-all}" ;;
    status|ps) cmd_status ;;
    metrics) cmd_metrics "${1:-all}" ;;
    logs) (( $# >= 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw logs WORKSPACE [OPTIONS]"; local logs_box="$1"; shift; cmd_logs "$logs_box" "$@" ;;
    exec) (( $# >= 2 )) || fatal "usage: msw exec WORKSPACE COMMAND..."; local exec_box="$1"; shift; cmd_exec "$exec_box" "$@" ;;
    disk) cmd_disk "${1:-all}" ;;
    resize) (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "usage: msw resize WORKSPACE MEMORY [CPUS]"; cmd_resize "$1" "$2" "${3:-}" ;;
    clean) cmd_clean "$@" ;;
    upgrade) cmd_upgrade "${1:-all}" ;;
    update) cmd_update ;;
    check) cmd_check "$@" ;;
    host)
      [[ "${1:-}" == repair && $# == 1 ]] || fatal "usage: msw host repair"
      cmd_host_repair
      ;;
    __github-verify-transaction)
      (( $# >= 2 && $# <= 3 )) || fatal "internal GitHub verification arguments missing"
      [[ "${MSW_GITHUB_VERIFY_INHERITED:-0}" == 1 ]] || fatal "internal GitHub verification lock missing"
      "$LOCKF_BIN" -s -t 0 9 >/dev/null 2>&1 || fatal "internal GitHub verification lock missing"
      cmd_github_verify "$1" "$2" "${3:-}" 1
      ;;
    backup) (( $# <= 1 )) || fatal "usage: msw backup [DIRECTORY]"; cmd_backup "${1:-$MSW_BACKUP_DIR}" ;;
    restore) cmd_restore "$@" ;;
    *) fatal "unknown command '$command'; run: msw help" ;;
  esac
}

if [[ "${MSW_SOURCE_ONLY:-0}" != 1 ]]; then
  main "$@"
fi

{"summary":"Design proposal: Use a normal, resumable onboarding window for installation and GitHub configuration; reserve the menu-bar popover for steady-state monitoring. First run explains the three trust-isolated workspaces, checks Apple Silicon, disk/RAM, network, tools, and permissions, then presents a phased installer for host tools, MSW files, MicroSandbox diagnostics, privileged loopback/hosts setup, base-image creation, workspace creation, and deep verification. Each phase shows progress, expandable logs, its effect, and Retry/Resume/Copy Diagnostics; closing onboarding must not lose state. Privileged work should use an authorized helper, not a hidden sudo shell.

GitHub setup is a first-class wizard: select a workspace, sign in using GitHub’s device flow, display the code with Copy Code and Open GitHub, respect expiry and polling intervals, choose owner and repositories, choose read-only or host-push access, then select a safe verification repository. Before approval, visibly explain that guest access is read-only while the write credential remains in macOS Keychain. Verification maps directly to `msw github setup/verify`: store credentials, bind only guest-read access, clone, create a temporary commit, prove guest push rejection, prove the host-only push path when enabled, delete the branch, and confirm cleanup. Failure must identify the failed stage and whether previous credentials were restored or the workspace was quarantined. The current CLI accepts separate fine-grained PATs, while OAuth device tokens alone cannot preserve its per-workspace read/write boundary; production therefore needs either a GitHub App architecture that preserves separate repository-scoped credentials or a secure noninteractive `msw github setup` contract using pipes/XPC—never tokens in argv, environment, logs, or generic text fields.

After setup, show one calm template status icon with only an attention indicator for actionable degraded, stale, or failed states. Its 380–400 pt keyboard-navigable popover has a fixed header with aggregate health, data age, Refresh, Activity, Settings, and Quit, followed by fixed-order workspace cards for dev, playgrounds, and personal. Each card shows purpose, lifecycle/quarantine state, freshness, compact CPU/memory when running, and the best next action. Visible quick actions are Start when stopped; Open Terminal, Open in Zed, and the most recent site/repository when running; Retry or Diagnostics when unavailable. A labeled workspace-actions menu may contain Stop, Restart, ports, logs, pull, clone, resize, and maintenance, but primary state and recovery must remain visible.

Use a separate resizable detail window with a NavigationSplitView for Overview, Metrics, Logs, Repositories, Ports, GitHub Access, Activity, Backup, and Diagnostics. Stream metrics only while visible; make logs searchable, pausable, bounded, and copyable. Repository rows expose Open in Zed, Open Terminal, Pull, and reviewed Push. Push review must show workspace, repository path, branch, SHA, commits, fast-forward policy, and preserve the CLI’s `PUSH` confirmation; force-with-lease is a distinct higher-risk choice.

Long operations persist in Activity after the popover closes, showing named phases, elapsed time, cancellation when safe, output details, and actionable recovery. Preserve the last good snapshot on communication failure, label it Stale with its observation time, and offer Retry; never translate transport failure into Stopped. Distinguish Mac offline, GitHub unavailable, missing CLI/configuration, stopped VM, quarantine, and partial workspace failure. Monitoring, launch, and popover opening must never start a VM.

Settings contains General (launch at login via SMAppService, polling, appearance), Workspaces (resources and defaults), GitHub (account, repository scope, verify, rotate, remove), Integrations (Ghostty, Zed, favorite ports), Notifications, Diagnostics, Documentation, and About.
